arr.n: Origin: San Martino, Valmozzola (Nati 1859 atto 6, proven). She came four years before her daughter Marianna, so she is the first arrival of the Galli/Manfredi lines.
arr.s: Ellis Island passenger manifest, S.S. La Provence, Havre 16 Jun 1906, arr. New York 22 Jun 1906, lines 12-13 (Martina Galli, widow, 47; Veronica Feretti, 18), image ref. 731-128, FS/statueofliberty.org JFZV-Q6R / JFZV-Q6T

cls.s: Ellis Island manifest, S.S. La Provence, Havre 16 Jun 1906, arr. New York 22 Jun 1906, List 5, image ref. 731-128 (FS image ark 3:1:3Q9M-C95M-X9D5-4, viewed free via statueofliberty.org JFZV-Q6R, 18 Oct 2026). Printed sheet header: 'SALOON, CABIN, AND STEERAGE ALIENS MUST BE COMPLETELY MANIFESTED. THIS SHEET IS FOR STEERAGE PASSENGERS.' Martina is line 12 on this sheet (stamped ADMITTED).

fare.v: Roughly $30-$40 per adult, steerage from Continental European ports (figure reported Aug 1904; not specific to the French Line, Havre, or 1906)
fare.s: GG Archives, 'Immigrants and the Steamship Steerage Rate Wars - 1904', quoting a 'Liverpool Shipping Letter' of 25 Aug 1904: 'Continental passengers still have to pay $30 to $40' (https://www.ggarchives.com/OT/Steerage/ImmigrantsSteerageRateWars-1904.html, read 18 Oct 2026). No French Line steerage tariff for 1906 was found in free sources.

ph.cr: La Provence at Le Havre, 1906 postcard ("LE HAVRE - Le Transatlantique LA PROVENCE", postmarked Ste-Adresse 21 Jul 1906); anonymous publisher. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.
ph.n: CGT La Provence of 1906 (Commons category 'La Provence (ship, 1906)'; Wikidata Q674330 image), not the 1951 ship.

hl: A widow of 47, Martina Galli Ferretti crossed from Le Havre to New York on the liner La Provence, landing on 22 June 1906 with her 18-year-old daughter Veronica.
The manifest says she paid her own passage, carried $30, and was going to join a cousin, Girolamo Granelli, in New York.
She lived until 1953 and is buried in Calvary Cemetery, Queens.

facts.t: Arrived New York 22 Jun 1906 on La Provence from Le Havre, a widow aged 47, 'h'keeper', paying her own passage, with $30, travelling with her daughter Veronica (18), to join her cousin Girolamo Granelli in New York
facts.s: Ellis Island passenger manifest, S.S. La Provence, Havre 16 Jun 1906, arr. New York 22 Jun 1906, lines 12-13 (Martina Galli; Veronica Feretti), image ref. 731-128, statueofliberty.org arrival-details JFZV-Q6R / JFZV-Q6T

arr.n: Origin: San Siro no. 10, Valmozzola, Parma (birth act Nati 1886 atto 12, proven). Ellis Island was closed after its June 1897 fire, so a late-1899 New York arrival would have been processed at the Barge Office (general knowledge; not from his papers).
arr.s: His own declaration of intention no. 75847, NY County Supreme Court, 25 Nov 1913 (FS QPZR-KJBD): came from Havre on La Gascogne, arrived New York 12 Nov 1899; same voyage in later naturalization papers (SDNY petition 60233). Manifest NOT found: the 13 Nov 1899 La Gascogne index has no Chiesa, so this is self-reported, not manifest-proven.

cls.s: No manifest found, so no record states his class. Reasoning only: he was 13, from San Siro, Valmozzola, arriving Nov 1899; his declaration of intention no. 75847 (1913, FS QPZR-KJBD) gives ship and date but no class, and most Italian emigrants of the time traveled steerage (general knowledge, not a record).

arr.fareN: No free source found for a French Line Havre-New York steerage fare in or near 1899; left null.

hl: Giuseppe (Joseph) Chiesa was born at San Siro in Valmozzola, Italy, in 1886 and spent his working life in New York kitchens.
In 1918 he was a cook at the Knickerbocker Club, a private gentlemen's club at Fifth Avenue and 62nd Street. His death certificate in 1946 calls him a chef.

cls.s: Ellis Island manifest, S.S. Chicago, Havre 16 Oct 1910, arr. New York 25 Oct 1910, NARA T715 roll 1584, List 17, images 281-282 (FS image arks 3:1:3Q9M-C9T3-5HR5-5 and -5HRP-F, viewed free via statueofliberty.org JJDL-QM3, 18 Oct 2026). The verso of List 17 (image 282) is printed 'THIS SHEET IS FOR STEERAGE PASSENGERS.' On the same voyage, second-cabin passengers are on a separately headed sheet (List 5, image 194: 'THIS SHEET IS FOR SECOND-CABIN PASSENGERS.'). The sheet's class is proven; rated probable only because line 17 is still a working identification of Marianna.

arr.fareN: No free source gives the 1910 French Line Havre-New York steerage fare. Context only, not her fare: a Swiss agency contract for Theodule Vial on this same sailing (Chicago, Havre 15/16 Oct 1910) cost 580 francs for rail Geneva-Havre (3rd class) plus the crossing, with $39.60 for New York-Denver rail; the contract says 'II class' on the Chicago and Vial is on the second-cabin sheet (List 5, line 25, image 193-194), so this is a second-cabin through fare, not steerage (GG Archives, https://www.ggarchives.com/OT/Contracts/Chicago-CGTFrenchLine-Contract-1910-10-12.html, which labels it third class).
arr.phN: No confirmed public-domain or CC image of the CGT Chicago (1908, later Guyane) was found on Wikimedia Commons. Commons 'Category:Chicago (ship, 1908)' shows a different ship (a Seattle halibut steamer).

Mar 1973 - still hypothesis; not in Ferrari/Galli household in 1950 census ED 31-2064 | Alive 5 Jul 1946: husband's death cert lists him as married to Mary (not widowed). | Birth date per the birth act (atto 34): 5 May 1885 (Valmozzola Nati 1885 no. 34, the day reads 'cinque' of the current month in an act dated May 1885), rated proven. Earlier readings of the act ('venticinque', read as 25 Apr 1885) and her US papers (25 Apr 1886; SSDI 25 Apr 1885) had suggested 25 April.

Conflict: RESOLVED 18 Oct 2026: date per the birth act (atto 34), 5 May 1885. Was: birth day. The copy of Nati 1885 atto 34 reads the day as 'cinque' (5) 'del corrente mese' in an act dated 9 [or 8] May 1885, giving 5 May 1885. Possible reading: 25 Apr 1885 (earlier reading 'venticinque'; US papers/SSDI 25 Apr), kept as birth.previous_reading. A 25th 'of the current month' cannot be right in an act dated early May, so 5 May 1885 is the stronger reading, unless the clerk meant April. | v10: age 29 on the 21 Oct 1915 marriage certificate fits a 1886 birth (her US papers) rather than May 1885 (she would have been 30). | v10: Eugenio Ferretti is 39 in the 1885 act, but his birth act (31 Aug 1847) makes him 37.

hl: Aldo Chiesa, born in East Harlem in 1920, served in the U.S. Army from 1944 to 1946. He was posted to the Hampton Roads Port of Embarkation at Newport News.
There he met Betty Ann Burkett at a USO dance, and they married in May 1945.
The Army's enlistment record shows Aldo was drafted in New York City in January 1944. He had three years of high school and worked as a skilled mechanic.

hl: Peter Samuel Burkett started out as a civil engineer in the West Virginia coalfields. He was living at Iroquois when he married Hattie Belle Rucker at Matoaka on 19 December 1923.
He later became a Methodist minister and served as pastor at Oak Grove in Madison County, Virginia, where he is buried.
The Daily Press of Newport News, where his daughter's family lived, printed his obituary on 31 July 1985.

news.t: Conference memoir: born Tazewell Co., Va., 21 Feb 1904, son of Peter Tolbert Burkett and Rose Belle Stevenson Burkett; Lynchburg College graduate; Conference course of study at Duke and Candler. Married Hattie Belle Rucker 19 Dec 1923 (married 57 years; she died 1 Mar 1981); five daughters, including Betty Ann Chiesa. Car repairman in the W.Va. coal mines, Maytag salesman, American Furniture Co. finisher, ran Burkett's Grocery in Martinsville; moved to Hampton 1942 as a shipfitter at Newport News Shipbuilding. Entered the ministry Oct 1948 from Copeland Methodist Church; whole ministry on the Charlottesville District: Schuyler (2 yrs), Greene (4), Bethlehem (8), Madison (12), and after retirement North Madison (6). Served on the Madison Co. Board of Supervisors. Remarried 1981. Died 29 Jul 1985; funeral at Madison UMC; buried in the cemetery at Madison. (Header '1904-1984' is a misprint; text gives 29 Jul 1985.)

hl: Hattie Belle Rucker married Peter Samuel Burkett at Matoaka, West Virginia, on 19 December 1923.

Through her mother, Cora Witten, she descended from the Witten family of Mercer County. The tree traces her Rucker line, through several probable links, back to the immigrant Peter Rucker, who was naturalized in Virginia in 1704.
Her obituary ran in the Daily Press on 3 March 1981.

hl: Betty Ann Burkett came to Newport News in 1942 to work in the shipyard during World War II. She met Aldo Chiesa at a USO dance, and they married in May 1945.
She graduated from Martinsville High School and Roanoke Business College and later retired from the personnel office at Fort Eustis.
A lifelong Methodist, she worked from 1985 on to raise support for the Henry Fork Service Center, which helps rural children in Virginia.

hl: Irvin Octavas Howell was born in North Carolina in 1887. He married Essie Mae Corbett in Gates County, North Carolina, in 1912.
The family later moved to Newport News, Virginia, where he died in 1985 at the age of 97.
His Daily Press obituary ran on 18 April 1985. He is buried in Peninsula Memorial Park.
The 1900 census confirms Irvin's siblings: Annie, John, Pattie and Caddie. He was the youngest of the five.

ev.t: Confederate cavalryman: enlisted 10 Jun 1861 at Tappahannock in Capt. Richard S. Cauthorn's company (Essex Light Dragoons), later Co. F, 9th Virginia Cavalry; age 23, farmer (one card: 'mechanic'); his horse valued at $130. Carried 'present' on rolls through Mar-Oct 1864.
Identity of the soldier with Irene's father: same name, birth (age 23 in Jun 1861 = born c. 1837-38), county and enlistment place; his letter of 1903 confirms Oct 1837.

CSR musters (Jun 1861-Oct 1864), mostly present. Absences: picket at Locust Grove Dec 1861, sick in camp Feb 1862, picket at Layton's Apr 1862, and detailed 21 Oct 1863 to carry home the horses of men killed and wounded. No hospital, capture or parole cards.
Context: 'Wm W. Dishman & Mary his wife who was Mary Dishman', daughter of David Dishman (d. 18 Apr 1866, Essex). This is the couple named as the candidate Lewis's parents in the hypothesis.

Married Mary E. (Lizzie) Watts, 12 Feb 1868, Essex Co.; groom 30, 'son of Wm. W. Dishman and Mary R. Dishman' (Virginia marriage abstract; Wilkerson index p. 82, Book 1 p. 20). Fits the 1900 census 'married 32 years'.
1880: listed as W. L. Dishman, 42, with wife Mary E. 30 and daughter Irene 2, Occupacia District, Essex Co.

Children (1880/1900 censuses, with dates from the compiled genealogy): Clarence Mercer (1868), Lewis (c. 1873), Sarah Jane (1875), Mary Irene (1877), Robert Clark (1880), Cleveland Sanford (1883), twins Allie Garnett and Annie Maguire (19 Oct 1887), William Henry (1895).
1900: Lewis Dishman, head, 63, born Oct 1837 Va., married 32 years (so married c. 1867-68), Occupacia, Essex Co.; wife Mary E. 51; daughter Irene 23.

W. L. Dishman of Pedro, Essex Co., veteran's pension application dated 25 May 1900: served 9th Va. Cavalry (company letter unclear); disability infirmities of age, rheumatism, loss of sight in right eye, tumor on left arm. Approved by Essex Co. court 18 Jun 1900, $15/yr. Statement sworn 15 Jul 1902: about 64, blind in one eye.

His own letter from Pedro, Essex Co., 10 Jun 1903: 'W. L. Dishman was born Oct 1837, who married a Miss Watts, was a son of W. W. Dishman who [was] born 1813, who married a Miss Dishman' - tracing the family back through Samuel Dishman (m. Miss Gray) and David Dishman (m. Miss Renolds). (The full name 'William Lewis' is probable, not proven: no record seen spells it out; see military.identification.)
Lived at Pedro (Occupacia district), Essex Co., in 1903; died about 1909 (compiled).
The Free Lance (Fredericksburg, Va.): Published roster of Company F, 9th Virginia Cavalry, lists 'H. Dishman, J. P. Dishman, W[m]. L. Dishman' together. Names 'Wm. L. Dishman'.

Named as father ('Lewis Dishman, born Essex Co.') on his daughter Irene Bruce's 1941 death certificate, with her mother Elizabeth Watts. His wife's maiden name Watts is proven; her first name 'Mary' is from the census 'Mary E.'.

stories.title: The 1966 Warwick Boulevard crash
stories.t: Before dawn on 22 Sep 1966, Louis Hicks left his home on Maxwell Lane in Newport News at about 5:15am to make business deliveries. His wife Evelyn watched him turn on his lights as he pulled out of the driveway. On a slight curve of Warwick Boulevard, 384 feet north of Oyster Point Road, his sedan delivery truck ran into the rear of a Hagan Truck Line tractor-trailer driven by Marvin H. Bryant. It was loaded with logs that stuck out six or seven feet past the trailer bed and was stopped partly in the northbound lane. Witnesses said they saw no lights burning on the back of the truck and no flares. A police officer saw three lights burning 'very dimly' on the trailer bed, and a string of lights on the logs was dark, with several broken. Louis was still alive when a milk-truck driver and a police officer tried to free him from behind the wheel, but he died of his injuries. Evelyn, as his widow and executrix, sued the trucking company and the driver for wrongful death. A jury in the Hustings Court of Newport News awarded her $40,000, and the Supreme Court of Virginia affirmed the judgment on 20 Jan 1969.

facts.t: Killed in a road accident on 22 Sep 1966, about 5:30 a.m., before daylight, on Warwick Boulevard, Newport News, 384 feet north of Oyster Point Road. The sedan delivery truck he was driving north hit the rear of a log-laden tractor-trailer of Hagan Truck Line (driver Marvin H. Bryant) that was stopped or barely moving in the lane with poor rear lights; the logs stuck out 6-7 feet behind the trailer. He was still alive under the wheel when help arrived. He had left home on Maxwell Lane about 5:15 a.m. to make business deliveries.

facts.t: Identification: the opinion names 'Louis Hicks' (the spelling on his stone), killed 22 Sep 1966 in Newport News, widow 'Evelyn Hicks'. That is his exact death date and city, and Find a Grave gives his wife as Evelyn Amelia Eagle (m. 1937). It also fits the family story that Virginia's brother died in a car wreck.

Obituary notice in the Daily Press, 23 Sep 1966 p. 10 (indexed as 'Hicks, Louis Richard')

Killed in a road accident on 22 Sep 1966, about 5:30 a.m., before daylight, on Warwick Boulevard, Newport News, 384 feet north of Oyster Point Road. The sedan delivery truck he was driving north hit the rear of a log-laden tractor-trailer of Hagan Truck Line (driver Marvin H. Bryant) that was stopped or barely moving in the lane with poor rear lights; the logs stuck out 6-7 feet behind the trailer. He was still alive under the wheel when help arrived. He had left home on Maxwell Lane about 5:15 a.m. to make business deliveries.

Identification: the opinion names 'Louis Hicks' (the spelling on his stone), killed 22 Sep 1966 in Newport News, widow 'Evelyn Hicks'. That is his exact death date and city, and Find a Grave gives his wife as Evelyn Amelia Eagle (m. 1937). It also fits the family story that Virginia's brother died in a car wreck.
A witness at the 1966 crash scene named Ralph Howell testified at trial. Whether he was related to the Howell family in this tree is not known; no kinship is asserted.

His widow Evelyn Hicks, executrix of his estate, sued for wrongful death in the Hustings Court of Newport News (Judge Conway H. Sheild Jr.). The jury awarded $40,000, and the Supreme Court of Virginia affirmed on 20 Jan 1969.

facts.t: FAMILY CLAIM: her husband was President William Howard Taft's grandson. VERDICT: NOT SUPPORTED. The records point to a different, distantly related Taft family. The President's three children were Robert A. Taft (sons William Howard III, Robert Jr., Lloyd Bowers and Horace Dwight), Helen Taft Manning (daughters Helen Manning Hunter and Caroline Manning Cunningham) and Charles Phelps Taft II (seven children, including Seth and Peter Rawson Taft). No Kingsley is among them.
facts.s: Wikipedia articles 'Robert A. Taft', 'Helen Taft Manning', 'Charles Phelps Taft II' (read 18 Oct 2026); Wikipedia, 'Taft family', https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taft_family (secondary; read 18 Oct 2026)

facts.t: So the family story probably grew from a real link. Her husband was a grandson of Judge Frederick Lovett Taft of Cleveland and of Mary Alice Arter, and a son of a Chief Justice of Ohio and U.S. Senator. That family is only distantly related to the President's: both descend from the colonial immigrant Robert Taft Sr. of Mendon/Uxbridge, Mass. (Wikipedia, secondary). A distant cousin, not a grandson.

hl: Raleigh F. Burkett left the Tazewell coalfields and went west. By 1940 he was living in Lyon County, Nevada, and working as a blacksmith.

On 22 October 1940, more than a year before Pearl Harbor, he joined the Regular Army in San Francisco for the Medical Department in the Panama Canal Zone. He later reached the rank of Technician 5th Grade and was buried in the Nevada veterans' cemetery in 1993.

hl: Walker Howard Rucker, born in Amherst (or Campbell) County, Virginia, moved to the Pocahontas coalfield. He was a 'railroader' when he married Cora Witten on Christmas Day 1890; family tradition says he built roads and bridges for the coal railroad.
By 1906 a newspaper called him 'a prominent contractor of Gary'.
Family tradition, not yet confirmed by a record, says he went back into a mine after an explosion and rescued two men.

facts.t: Family story: as a mine 'cut boss' he went back into a mine after an explosion and saved two men, and suffered afterwards from 'black damp'

H. Rucker, died at Welch, W. Va. and was buried here last Sunday week.' Both parents dead by 1925 fits Walker (d. 1921) and Cora (d. 1913); daughter Gertrude also married a Maloney. Also CVN 15 Aug 1919 p. 4 (Graham): 'Miss Mary Rucker has returned from a two weeks visit to her sister, at Gary.' Needs a WV death record (Welch, McDowell Co., Jan 1925) to confirm.

b.d: c. Jan 1753 ('aged 80 years in the month of January next', Oct 1832)

hl: Thomas Witten Jr. served as an ensign and frontier scout ('Indian spy') during the Revolution. In old age he drew a federal pension for that service.
The county historian William Pendleton says he was one of Tazewell County's first members of the Virginia General Assembly, sitting in 1801-02 and 1802-03.

Thomas Witten's pension says he was an ensign of frontier scouts. The Washington County court's minutes back this up: on 26 February 1777, at one of the county's first sessions, it recommended him to the Governor as an ensign of militia.

facts.t: Son of Thomas Witten (first settler) & Elizabeth Cecil; one of five unmarried sons brought to the Clinch 1767; ensign; Tazewell delegate 1801-02 and 1802-03; m. his cousin Eleanor Cecil
facts.s: William C. Pendleton, History of Tazewell County and Southwest Virginia 1748-1920 (Richmond, 1920), pp. 401-405 'The Wittens and Cecils', archive.org/details/historyoftazewel00pend_0 (county history; no record citations) pp. 402-403

facts.t: His pension witnesses William Cecil and Nancy Cecil (1832) fit Pendleton's William Cecil (son of Samuel) who m. Ann Witten (Thomas Sr.'s daughter), i.e. his sister and brother-in-law
facts.s: S6407 declaration  + William C. Pendleton, History of Tazewell County and Southwest Virginia 1748-1920 (Richmond, 1920), pp. 401-405 'The Wittens and Cecils', archive.org/details/historyoftazewel00pend_0 (county history; no record citations) p. 404

facts.t: Represented Tazewell Co. in the Virginia General Assembly with David Ward at the sessions of 1801-02 and 1802-03 (among the county's first members)
facts.s: William C. Pendleton, History of Tazewell County and Southwest Virginia 1748-1920 (Richmond, 1920), archive.org/details/historyoftazewel00pend, p. 403 (county history; no record citation)

ev.t: c. Jan 1753 ('aged 80 years in the month of January next', Oct 1832)
Son of Thomas Witten (first settler) & Elizabeth Cecil; one of five unmarried sons brought to the Clinch 1767; ensign; Tazewell delegate 1801-02 and 1802-03; m. his cousin Eleanor Cecil
Ensign and frontier 'Indian spy' from 1776 to the end of the Revolutionary War; later a federal pensioner
Washington Co. court, 26 Feb 1777: 'Thomas Whitten' among the men recommended to the Governor as militia ensigns. This fits his own pension statement that he was an ensign from 5 Jun 1776
Represented Tazewell Co. in the Virginia General Assembly with David Ward at the sessions of 1801-02 and 1802-03 (among the county's first members)
His pension witnesses William Cecil and Nancy Cecil (1832) fit Pendleton's William Cecil (son of Samuel) who m. Ann Witten (Thomas Sr.'s daughter), i.e. his sister and brother-in-law

d.p: St. Mark's Parish, Orange Co., Virginia

arr.date: before 24 Apr 1704 (date of his naturalization petition)
arr.n: The rating covers only the fact that he was a foreign-born alien in Virginia by April 1704. Year, port, ship and origin are unknown. 'Settled about 1690', the James River shipwreck story and the Huguenot/German origins are family tradition (Wood 1932 p. 1; hypothesis). No European origin is proven; Y-DNA (R-A434) has no European match.
arr.s: H. R. McIlwaine, ed., Legislative Journals of the Council of Colonial Virginia, vol. 1 (1918), pp. 390-391 (24 Apr 1704, petition of Peter Rucker 'praying for Naturalizacon'); Journals of the House of Burgesses 1702/3-1712 (1912), pp. 48, 74 (8 May 1704, naturalization agreed); archive.org

hl: Peter Rucker, the immigrant ancestor of the Virginia Ruckers, asked the colony's Council and House of Burgesses to naturalize him in April 1704. The House agreed on 8 May 1704.
His homeland is still unknown. His own petition never calls him a French refugee, and his male-line DNA has not yet matched any Rucker family in Europe.

facts.t: Naturalization: a petition 'for Naturalization of Peter Ruckes' was read in the House of Burgesses on 24 Apr 1704. On 8 May 1704 the House agreed to the committee report on the petitions of John Gill, Stephen Gill, Samuel de Monville, Teleife Alverton, Isaac Garret, Peter Ruckes and Clypian Prou, finding it 'reasonable the said persons should be naturalized when they are qualifyed by taking the Oathes'. This confirms Wood's citation (Wood gives p. 74 and spells the name Rucker).
facts.s: H. R. McIlwaine, ed., Journals of the House of Burgesses of Virginia 1702/3-1705, 1705-1706, 1710-1712 (Richmond, 1912), pp. 48 (Mon. 24 Apr 1704) and 74 (Mon. 8 May 1704), archive.org/details/journalsofhouse06virg

facts.t: Origin unknown. He was naturalized with French-named petitioners (Huguenot/Alsace theories), but no record names his birthplace. The Rucker Family Society also states no evidence of origin. Arrival c.1700 is an inference from the 4-year residency rule.
facts.s: H. R. McIlwaine, ed., Journals of the House of Burgesses of Virginia 1702/3-1705, 1705-1706, 1710-1712 (Richmond, 1912), pp. 48 (Mon. 24 Apr 1704) and 74 (Mon. 8 May 1704), archive.org/details/journalsofhouse06virg; theruckerfamilysociety.org/peterrucker.html (pointer)

facts.t: Council journal, 24 Apr 1704: 'The petitions of Cyprian Prou, Peter Rucker, & Isaac Garret praying for Naturalizacon Were severally presented & read' and referred to the Burgesses. Entered separately from the Veillon group petition and from the Manakin French refugee papers. Not called a French refugee. Wood 1932's quotation merging him with Veillon et al. is a conflation.
facts.s: H. R. McIlwaine, ed., Legislative Journals of the Council of Colonial Virginia, vol. 1 (Richmond, 1918), p. 390-391 (Mon. 24 Apr 1704), archive.org/details/legislativejourn01virg

facts.t: Not named in the 12 May 1705 act naturalizing the Manakin French refugees (Hening 3:228 title; text in Winfree 1971 pp. 39-41, read via web transcription). No 1704 naturalization act exists in Hening 3:224-226. The naturalization rests on the 8 May 1704 House resolution, conditional on taking the oaths. Oath-taking not yet found.

hl: Pendleton's 1920 county history calls Thomas Witten the first white man to settle with his family inside present-day Tazewell County. He arrived at the 'Crabapple Orchard' on the Clinch River in the spring of 1767.
When trouble with Native Americans began around 1772-73, he and his sons built a stockade, Witten's Fort, where neighbors took refuge.

A 1787 Montgomery County deed shows Thomas Witten and his son-in-law John Greenup jointly buying 200 acres on the Clinch River for £5. The two men had led the first families into the Crab Orchard country in 1771.
Family tradition, printed in 1922, says Thomas was born in Maryland in 1719 and kept a written family record in 1766. That record has not been found.

hl: James Witten was born in Maryland in 1759 and grew up on the Clinch frontier. Bickley wrote that by about fifteen he was already 'much distinguished as a hunter and woodsman'.

In 1779 he was made constable of Captain Maxwell's militia company. From 1794 to 1796 he served as a paid scout against Indian raids. 'When any duty requiring bravery, firmness, and prudence had to be performed, James Witten was the man invariably chosen.'

facts.t: Not a son of President Taft. His parents were Frederick Lovett Taft and Mary Alice Arter. Wikipedia calls him a 'distant relative' of the famous Taft family and 'sixth cousin once removed' of Senator Robert A. Taft (the President's son), unsourced. The 'Taft family' article places him among the descendants of Robert Taft Jr. (b. 1674), son of the immigrant Robert Taft Sr. of Mendon/Uxbridge, Mass. The President's line also comes from Robert Taft Sr. (via Aaron and Peter Rawson Taft of Uxbridge). The exact cousin degree is not verified here.

Amherst College A.B. 1925; Harvard LL.B. 1928. Partner at Dustin, McKeehan, Merrick, Arter & Stewart (later Arter & Hadden). Ohio House 1933-34. U.S. Senator from Ohio Nov 1946 to Jan 1947 (Burton's unexpired term). Justice of the Ohio Supreme Court from 1949 and Chief Justice 1963-70; he wrote 609 opinions and dissented in State v. Married Louise Dakin on 14 Sep 1927. They had four sons: Charles, Kingsley, Sheldon and David.

The Tidewater Science Congress named her Science Educator of the Year in 1996.

stories.title: Peter Rucker: The Immigrant Who Asked to Become English
stories.summary: In 1704 a foreign-born planter petitioned Virginia's House of Burgesses to be naturalized. Who was he, and where did he come from?
stories.html:
Peter Rucker is the earliest proven ancestor of our Rucker line, yet he still keeps most of his secrets. ## A petition in Williamsburg The first record of Peter comes from the spring of 1704. On Monday, 24 April, the governor's Council in Williamsburg read "the petitions of Cyprian Prou, Peter Rucker, & Isaac Garret praying for Naturalizacon." They sent them on to the House of Burgesses. On 8 May 1704 a committee reported on his petition and those of John Gill, Stephen Gill, Samuel de Monville, Teleife Alverton, Isaac Garret and Cyprian Prou. Its finding was that it was "reasonable the said persons should be naturalized when they are qualifyed by taking the Oathes Enjoyned by Law." The House agreed. Naturalization was only needed by someone born outside the English crown's dominions. So we can say with confidence that Peter was a foreigner. He was most likely born somewhere in continental Europe. ## French refugee, or something else? Family tradition, recorded in 1932, says Peter was a French Huguenot who was shipwrecked near the mouth of the James River and swam ashore. The journals do not support the Huguenot part as firmly as older books suggest. The Council recorded the petitions of the French refugees at Manakin Town as a separate matter. Peter's petition was entered separately, with two other individuals. He is never called a refugee. His name is also missing from the 1705 act that naturalized the Manakin settlers. His surname looks Germanic, and one London expert of the 1930s thought it German or Dutch. Searches of Walloon and German Huguenot records have found nothing. ## What his DNA says Male-line descendants who have tested with the Rucker Family DNA Project share a distinctive Y-DNA lineage, R-A434. It belongs to a western European branch called DF27. So far it does not match the German Rucker families who have tested, and no match has turned up in Europe. Peter's homeland therefore remains an open question. ## A planter on the Rappahannock By 1704 Peter held 500 acres in Essex County. In January 1707/8 Frederick and Sarah Coghill leased land on Cockleshell Creek to Peter and his wife Elizabeth. The same day they deeded it to his son John, with his sons Peter and Thomas next in line. He later moved west to St. Mark's Parish in Orange County. There he made his will on 18 January 1743/4, signing with his mark. He left his estate to his wife Elizabeth for life, with bequests to his children Thomas, Elizabeth Pierce, William, Mary Offell, James, Ephraim, Ann Cook and Margaret Tinsley. The will was proved on 23 February 1743/4. ## What we do not know No record names Peter's parents, his birthplace or the year he arrived. Online trees that give him a father named Ambrose Rucker, a mother named Elizabeth Beauchamp, or a birthplace in Bavaria cite no original records. They should be treated as unproven. ## Sources - H. R. McIlwaine, ed., Legislative Journals of the Council of Colonial Virginia, vol. 1 (Richmond, 1918), p. 390-391, 24 Apr 1704. archive.org/details/legislativejourn01virg
